routes.description: Establish that human beings possess a limited but genuine volitional capacity to regulate conscious attention, activate reason, and thereby influence deliberation and action without claiming unrestricted control over mental content, circumstances, or outcomes.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if regulating awareness is directly supportable as an agent-caused, non-necessitated capacity that changes deliberative engagement and cannot be exhaustively redescribed as compelled inference, strongest-desire operation, randomness, or mechanical event causation.

motionBridge.description: Show that voluntary regulation of conscious focus and rational engagement constitutes free will under the motion's volitional-capacity alternative.

centralBridges.description: Precisely distinguish choosing the degree and method of conscious engagement from choosing every thought, desire, conclusion, action, or outcome.
Explain how a person can cause a choice to focus without that choice being necessitated by prior events or reduced to a causeless random occurrence.
Ground the claimed capacity in awareness of modulating attention, including the ability to sustain focus, broaden context, or evade recognized considerations.
Connect chosen cognitive engagement to changes in deliberation, value ordering, operative desires, and consequent conduct.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Support a conception of consciousness and causation broad enough to permit volitional agency rather than assuming an exclusively mechanical model.
Account for coercion, bodily processes, unchosen emotions, and environmental limits while preserving the narrower claimed control over awareness.

routes.description: Deny both ultimate control and the proposed capacity to activate reason by showing that actions, attention, desires, and convictions arise through determining influences or indeterminacy, neither of which makes the person the controlling author.
routes.successCriteria: The route succeeds if the proposed act of focusing remains unexplained outside determination or randomness, while introspection, deliberation, evasion, regret, and coercive choice can be accounted for without an independent volitional power.

motionBridge.description: Show that neither ultimate authorship nor voluntary control of rational focus survives the alternatives of causal determination and indeterminacy.

centralBridges.description: Apply the determined-or-random dilemma to actions and mental events, including the purported agent-caused decision to activate awareness.
Explain attention, arising considerations, rational conviction, and action through unchosen influences rather than proactive selection by a chooser.
Account for conduct, evasion, self-modification, and value-sensitive deliberation through first-order and higher-order desires whose operative strength is not freely chosen.
Establish that an immediate experience of agency does not by itself settle whether the apparent control is genuine or instead admits an alternative explanation.

subsidiaryBridges.description: Test libertarian control by asking what could explain divergent choices under otherwise identical relevant conditions.
Keep the conceptual objection applicable whether consciousness is characterized as material, immaterial, or emergent.

sections.title: The Scope and Locus of the Claimed Freedom
sections.rationale: The motion permits either ultimate control or a volitional capacity, making the definition of freedom and the distinction between control of attention, mental content, action, and outcome foundational to both burdens.

sections.title: Causation, Randomness, and Agent Authorship
sections.rationale: The central metaphysical clash concerns whether determination and indeterminacy exhaust the possibilities or whether an agent can cause a non-necessitated choice without converting it into randomness.

sections.title: Introspection, Experience, and Evidence of Control
sections.rationale: The positive case relies substantially on awareness of changing one's mental engagement, while the skeptical burden requires explaining why that experience may not establish the interpretation of genuine control.

sections.title: Reason, Desire, and the Mechanics of Deliberation
sections.rationale: Whether focus can be voluntarily activated and alter value-sensitive conduct, or whether considerations, convictions, and strongest desires govern the entire process, directly determines the viability of the motion's narrower alternative.

sections.title: Consciousness, Constraints, and Applied Choice
sections.rationale: Accounts of mind, coercion, bodily limits, emotion formation, regret, and evasion test whether the competing causal models remain coherent when applied beyond abstract choice examples.

chunk-001:chunk001-c03.proposition: Causation does not entail necessitation by prior events, so treating every caused occurrence as predetermined improperly collapses two distinct concepts.

chunk-001:chunk001-c04.proposition: People can introspectively observe themselves regulating mental effort and choosing whether to activate reason, drift, or evade, evidencing the relevant volitional capacity.

chunk-001:chunk001-c05.proposition: Free will is the capacity to activate and use the rational faculty, rather than a power to select every mental content, action, or outcome.

chunk-001:chunk001-c06.proposition: A person can consider broader values and originate a choice caused by the agent without that choice being random or necessitated by prior factors.

chunk-002:chunk002-c01.proposition: Free will selects the method of conscious engagement rather than subconscious content, allowing chosen rational focus to affect which desire ultimately governs action.

chunk-002:chunk002-c07.proposition: Human consciousness is a real nonphysical existent whose rational faculty operates by choice, making a purely material and mechanistic account of human agency incomplete.

chunk-002:chunk002-c09.proposition: Although present emotions are not directly chosen, repeated choices to think can revise value judgments and thereby shape emotional dispositions and operative desires over time.

chunk-002:chunk002-c10.proposition: The observable capacity to evade recognized facts shows that rational evidence does not compel acceptance and supplies direct introspective evidence of free will.

chunk-004:chunk004-c02.proposition: External force can sharply restrict available actions and obstruct a person's exercise of rational judgment and free will without disproving the underlying volitional capacity.

chunk-004:chunk004-c03.proposition: The fundamental volitional choice is whether and how fully to activate one's mind, with degrees ranging from full-context awareness to evasion or drift.

chunk-001:chunk001-c01.proposition: Neither causal determination nor indeterminacy permits a person to be the ultimate author or controller of an action.

chunk-001:chunk001-c07.proposition: The felt immediacy of an experience cannot establish its interpretation, because introspection can present illusory forces or agencies as real.

chunk-001:chunk001-c08.proposition: Attention to deliberation reveals thoughts, options, and rational conclusions presenting themselves rather than being proactively selected by a chooser.

chunk-001:chunk001-c09.proposition: Agent causation does not end the explanatory regress, because conscious actions follow unchosen desires and the strongest operative desire governs behavior.

chunk-002:chunk002-c06.proposition: Agent causation does not explain control because a mental event either has determining causes beyond the agent's ultimate control or occurs causelessly and randomly.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-04.proposition: Libertarian free will requires a genuine ability to act differently in physically identical circumstances, for which no differentiating explanation is available.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-09.proposition: Introspective confidence in free will is defeasible when philosophical considerations provide alternative explanations of the apparent experience.

chunk-003:chunk003-candidate-10.proposition: The alternate-possibilities conception of free will is philosophically incoherent regardless of whether consciousness is material, immaterial, or emergent.

chunk-004:chunk004-c08.proposition: Even conscious conduct under coercion remains technically a choice between desire-governed alternatives, although ordinary language reasonably describes it as forced.
